summary: This proposed standard defines a TRILL IS-IS application sub-TLV that lets a TRILL switch report sets of addresses. Each set contains all the addresses that identify the same interface and also names the TRILL switch through which that interface can be reached.

eli5.summary: This lets a network switch publish a list saying that these several addresses all belong to the same network port, and which switch it can be reached through.

questions: what is the trill interface addresses appsub-tlv
what is a trill ia appsub-tlv template
how does trill avoid arp flooding
subtitle: A compact IS-IS record that says which MAC, IPv4 and IPv6 addresses belong to one interface and which TRILL switch reaches it.

tldr.problem: A TRILL network has no compact way to report that several addresses of different kinds, such as a MAC, an IPv4 and an IPv6 address, all designate the same interface and which TRILL switch it sits behind.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7961 defines the Interface Addresses (IA) APPsub-TLV, which carries a Template describing the address types, then a list of Address Sets that follow that Template, plus optional sub-sub-TLVs for sizes, fixed addresses, Data Labels and topology.
tldr.outcome: The information can be used to synthesize replies to, or avoid the need for, ARP, IPv6 Neighbor Discovery or flooding of unknown MAC addresses, and to discard frames with forged source addresses when the data is complete.

today: RFC 7961 is a Proposed Standard and the data shows no obsoleting or updating RFC, so it remains the definition of the TRILL Interface Addresses APPsub-TLV.

sections.title: What the IA APPsub-TLV Is For
sections.content:
RFC 7961 specifies an IS-IS application sub-TLV (APPsub-TLV) for TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links, defined in RFC 6325). It lets a TRILL switch report sets of addresses where every address in a set designates the same interface (port). For example, a 48-bit MAC address, an IPv4 address and an IPv6 address can be reported as all belonging to one interface.

Each set is also tied to a Data Label (a VLAN or a Fine-Grained Label, see RFC 7172) and to the TRILL switch, and optionally the TRILL switch port, from which the interface is reachable.

The RFC says this information could be used in some cases to synthesize responses to, or bypass the need for, ARP, IPv6 Neighbor Discovery (RFC 4861), RARP, or the flooding of unknown destination MAC addresses. If the information is complete, it can also help detect and discard packets with forged source addresses.

The sub-TLV appears inside the TRILL GENINFO TLV defined in the ESADI RFC (RFC 7357) but may also occur in other application contexts.
sections.eli5: Switches in a network need to know which door each device lives behind. This gives them a tidy way to say: these three addresses are one device, and here is the switch to reach it.

sections.title: The Fixed Fields
sections.content:
The IA APPsub-TLV starts with fixed fields, then a Template, then the Address Sets, then any sub-sub-TLVs. Its type is 10 (IA-SUBTLV). In an extended flooding scope TLV the Type and Length are 2-byte integers.

  • Length: variable, minimum 7. If it is 6 or less, or the sub-TLV runs past its enclosing TLV, it MUST be ignored.
  • Addr Sets End: 2 bytes giving the byte number of the last byte of the last Address Set. If it is greater than Length or points before the end of the Template, the sub-TLV is corrupt and MUST be discarded. If it equals Length there are no sub-sub-TLVs.
  • Nickname: the 16-bit identifier of the TRILL switch by which the sets are reachable. If 0, they are reachable from the switch that originated the message.
  • Flags: one byte. D means the data is directory information, L means it was learned locally by observing ingressed frames. Both can be set. Reserved bits MUST be sent as zero.
  • Confidence: 0 to 254, with 255 treated as 254.
sections.eli5: The front of the record is like the label on a folder: how long it is, which switch it belongs to, whether it was written down by hand or noticed along the way, and how sure the author is.

sections.title: Templates and Address Sets
sections.content:
The Template says what each Address Set looks like. Its first byte is an unsigned integer K.

  • K from 1 to 31: K Address Family Numbers (AFNs), 2 bytes each, follow and give the exact type and order of the addresses in every set.
  • K from 32 to 39: a one-byte shorthand for a well-known sequence, listed below. The 0x01 bit means an IPv4 address is present, 0x02 an IPv6 address, and 0x04 an RBridge Port ID.
  • K of 0 or 255: the whole sub-TLV is ignored. Values 40 to 254 are reserved, and if a receiver does not understand K, any Address Sets are ignored.

Every Address Set has exactly the sequence the Template names, packed with no padding. The same AFN may occur more than once in a Template, and the same address may appear in different sets, so a MAC address with three IPv6 addresses can be encoded either as one set with three IPv6 slots or as three sets that repeat the MAC. Which is smaller depends on how many interfaces share that pattern.

A receiver must know the size of each AFN in the Template, otherwise it MUST ignore the sub-TLV unless an AFN Size sub-sub-TLV supplies it. A device that only cares about some address types may ignore the rest.
sections.eli5: The Template is the column headings of a table, and each Address Set is one row. Everyone reads the headings first, so they know how to read each row.

sections.title: The Sub-sub-TLVs
sections.content:
After the Address Sets, the remaining bytes are parsed as sub-sub-TLVs, with no ordering restriction. Unknown types are ignored, and if parsing is impossible the whole IA APPsub-TLV is considered corrupt and ignored. Four types are defined:

  • AFN Size (type 1): 3-byte records of an AFN and the size in bytes of its addresses. It lets a receiver parse a Template that contains an AFN it does not know, or gives the size of a variable-length address. If a record disagrees with the size a switch already knows, the sub-TLV MUST be ignored.
  • Fixed Address (type 2): an AFN plus one address that counts as part of every Address Set, to save space. It is not listed in the Template.
  • Data Label (type 3): a Length of 2 carries a 12-bit VLAN ID, a Length of 3 carries an FGL. Several occurrences mean the interfaces are reachable in all of those labels.
  • Topology (type 4): a 12-bit topology number from RFC 5120.

In a non-extended LSP only 1-byte Types and Lengths are available, so types above 255 and lengths above 255 cannot be used there.
sections.eli5: Sub-sub-TLVs are sticky notes at the bottom of the record: how big a strange address is, one value shared by every row, which VLAN, which topology.

sections.title: Synthesizing Addresses from Pieces
sections.content:
Section 6 of the RFC describes extra AFNs that hold only part of an address: OUI (3 bytes, the first part of a MAC address), MAC/24 (the last 3 bytes of a 48-bit MAC), MAC/40 (the last 5 bytes of a 64-bit MAC), IPv6/64 (the first 8 bytes of an IPv6 address) and RBridge Port ID (16 bits, identifying a port on a TRILL switch).

Each Address Set, after adding any Fixed Address sub-sub-TLVs, is processed like this:

  • Each OUI is combined with each MAC/24 and each MAC/40. With K1 OUIs, K2 MAC/24s and K3 MAC/40s, K1*K2 48-bit and K1*K3 64-bit MAC addresses are produced. If there are no OUIs, the MAC/24 and MAC/40 entries are ignored, and the other way round.
  • Each IPv6/64 is combined with each 48-bit or 64-bit MAC, which supplies the lower 64 bits of the IPv6 address. A 48-bit MAC is first expanded to 64 bits as in RFC 7042. K4 prefixes and K5 MACs give K4*K5 IPv6 addresses. IPv6/64 entries with no MAC are ignored.

Synthesized addresses are treated as if they had been in the Address Set all along.
sections.eli5: Instead of writing a full address every time, you can write the shared beginning once and only the different endings in each row. The reader glues them back together.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The integrity of address mapping and reachability data, and the correctness of Data Labels, matter a great deal. Forged or incorrect data can deliver packets to the wrong party and violate security policy.

The RFC only describes a data format. It provides no mechanism to secure the data beyond a few consistency checks. Protection is left to whatever carries it: ESADI security (RFC 7357) or RBridge Channel (RFC 7178) channel tunnel security.

If the data is known to be complete and correct, a switch can discard native traffic whose source address should not be reachable from the receiving switch. The optional Port ID lets that filtering work per port. A counter of frames discarded this way should be kept for manageability.
sections.eli5: A wrong entry in the list could send a letter to the wrong house. This document only defines how to write the list, so protecting it is the job of whatever delivers it.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA allocated type 10 for the IA APPsub-TLV in the TRILL APPsub-TLV Types registry (name "IA"). It also allocated new Address Family Numbers: 16389 for 48-bit MAC, 16390 for 64-bit MAC, 16391 OUI, 16392 MAC/24, 16393 MAC/40, 16394 IPv6/64 and 16395 RBridge Port ID. Values 1 and 2 are IPv4 and IPv6.

A new sub-registry holds the sub-sub-TLV types, with Expert Review as the procedure. Types 0, 255 and 65535 are reserved, types 1 to 4 are the four defined here, and the rest are unassigned.
sections.eli5: IANA keeps the official phone book of numbers. This RFC asked for a number for the new record type and for each new kind of address piece.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
Appendix A gives two annotated examples. The simple one carries two sets of 48-bit MAC and IPv4 address, using Template 33. Each Address Set is 10 bytes (6 for the MAC, 4 for the IPv4 address), and the total size is 7 + 2*10 = 27.

The complex one uses Template 37 (MAC, IPv4, RBridge Port ID) with three sets, a Data Label sub-sub-TLV that gives an FGL overriding the surrounding message, and a Fixed Address sub-sub-TLV with an IPv6/64 prefix. Each MAC address is expanded by inserting 0xfffe after the OUI and inverting the local/global bit, and the result becomes the lower 64 bits of an IPv6 address.

The RFC notes the same data could use explicit AFNs instead of the shorthand, and that using an OUI plus MAC/24 values saves bytes only once there are more than three Address Sets.
sections.eli5: The examples show a real filled-in record, row by row, so you can check that you can read one yourself.

items.desc: Size in bytes of the addresses for an AFN.

items.desc: One address treated as part of every Address Set.
